subtitle: Recognize when an emphasis on sameness hides real cultural difference in your team's practice and your own habits, and take practical steps to hold commonality and difference together.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including policy and program staff, case managers, supervisors and leaders, who want shared language for the transitional orientation of the Intercultural Development Continuum. No prior course in the series is required.

lessons.title: Naming Minimization: commonality, universalism and a transitional mindset
objectives: Describe Minimization as the transitional orientation between monocultural and intercultural mindsets on the Intercultural Development Continuum.
Distinguish the two forms of commonality emphasis: human similarity and universal values.
Explain how emphasizing sameness can mask deeper cultural difference, and why it can also serve as a strategy for people in non-dominant groups.
Identify what this course will not do, including administering or guessing anyone's Intercultural Development Inventory result.
lessons.teaching:
This is the third course in the program's six-part series on the Intercultural Development Continuum, the model published by IDI, LLC that describes how people and groups make sense of cultural difference. The continuum moves from the more monocultural mindsets of Denial and Polarization, through the transitional orientation of Minimization, to the intercultural mindsets of Acceptance and Adaptation. The program's series adds a sixth course on Integration, a stage drawn from Milton Bennett's earlier Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity, on which the continuum builds. The word "transitional" matters. Minimization is not a failure and not a destination. It is a place many thoughtful people and many public organizations stand, and it carries real strengths along with real blind spots.

The continuum describes Minimization as highlighting commonalities in two ways. The first is similarity: the conviction that underneath it all, people share the same basic needs for safety, food, belonging and respect. The second is universalism: the belief that certain values and principles, such as fairness, honesty or individual rights, apply everywhere and can be used to judge any situation. Both beliefs contain truth. The difficulty is that emphasizing them can mask a deeper understanding of how culture shapes what those needs and values look like in practice. Bennett describes this orientation as assuming that one's own experience is shared by others, so that visible differences are treated as surface variations on themes that everyone supposedly holds in the same way.

The continuum also names two different sources of Minimization. For people whose culture shapes the rules of an institution, it can reflect limited cultural self-understanding: my way of doing things feels like no culture at all, just common sense. For people from non-dominant groups, emphasizing commonality can be a deliberate strategy for navigating values and practices set largely by the dominant group, and the continuum notes that this strategy can have survival value. These two forms look similar from the outside but come from very different places, which is one reason never to assume why a colleague talks about sameness.

Finally, a boundary. The Intercultural Development Inventory is a fifty-item assessment that can only be administered, and its results only shared, by a licensed Qualified Administrator. This course uses the continuum's language as a shared vocabulary for patterns in practice. It does not measure anyone, and nobody in this program should guess, announce or record a colleague's orientation. If you want to take the inventory, ask your supervisor or the program team about working with a Qualified Administrator.
lessons.keyPoint: Minimization emphasizes what people share, through similarity and universal principles. It is a transitional orientation with real strengths, but it can hide how culture shapes the ways people experience the same needs and values.
lessons.example: Fictional case: At a Disability Services Division planning meeting, Arne says the new person-centered planning guide needs no cultural review because "every family wants the same thing, a good life for their loved one." Keisha, who has worked with Hmong, Somali and Ojibwe families in her county partnerships, agrees with the goal but notices the guide assumes the person served will make decisions alone in a private meeting. In some families she has worked with, important decisions involve several relatives or elders. Nobody in the room disagrees that families want a good life. The question is whether the guide's process was built around one picture of how that happens.
lessons.question: What is the most useful thing Keisha could say next?
choices: Tell Arne that his comment shows he is stuck in Minimization and needs intercultural training.
Agree with the shared goal, then ask the group what assumptions the guide makes about who takes part in decisions and how it could invite each person to say who they want involved.
Stay quiet, since the shared goal is true and raising culture might slow the project down.
feedback: Labeling a colleague's orientation is exactly what this program does not do. It turns a practice question into a judgment about a person and usually ends the useful conversation.

This is the strongest response. It honors the real commonality, then moves to a concrete, checkable question about the process. Asking each person who they want involved avoids swapping one assumption for another.
The shared goal is true, but staying quiet leaves the hidden assumption in the guide. A short question now costs less than revising a guide after families find it does not fit.
lessons.reflection: Think about a time you said or thought "people are people" at work. What was true in that statement, and what might it have left out about how people actually experience the same need?
lessons.action: Pick one document you use often, such as a form, template or meeting agenda. Write down two assumptions it makes about how people communicate, decide or show up, and note whether those assumptions were ever checked with the people it serves.

check.question: According to the Intercultural Development Continuum, why is Minimization called a transitional orientation?
check.correct: Because it sits between the more monocultural mindsets of Denial and Polarization and the more intercultural mindsets of Acceptance and Adaptation.
wrong: Because people only stay in it for a short, fixed period of time before moving on.
Because it is the point at which people have finished learning about cultural difference.
check.feedback: Transitional describes position on the continuum, not duration or completion. Minimization moves past judging difference as a threat, but its focus on commonality can still hide how culture shapes experience. People and teams can remain there for a long time, and moving on is developmental work rather than a timetable.

lessons.title: Noticing Minimization in a team's default practice
objectives: Identify signs of commonality emphasis built into team routines, forms and policies rather than in individual attitudes.
Compare a uniform process that looks neutral with the cultural assumptions it carries.
Explain how treating one way of working as "just how it's done" can mask dominant culture patterns in an organization.
Draft a practice-focused question that surfaces a hidden assumption without blaming a colleague.
lessons.teaching:
Minimization is easiest to see not in what people believe but in what a team does by default. Teams build habits: how meetings run, how feedback is given, what a complete application looks like, what counts as professional. When those habits reflect one cultural pattern and are treated as simply neutral, the team is practicing a form of Minimization even if every member cares deeply about equity. Bennett makes a pointed observation about this at the organizational level: organizations in this orientation tend to exaggerate the benefits of unbiased equal opportunity, which can mask the continued operation of dominant culture privilege. The rules really are the same for everyone. The question is whose way of working the rules were written around.

Some common signals in public service work: "We treat everyone the same" offered as the full answer to a question about access. A notice or form tested only with staff. Meeting norms that reward quick verbal debate, so that people who wait for an opening or prefer to think before speaking rarely shape decisions. Hiring panels that score "communication" by one style of eye contact and self-promotion. Outreach plans that translate a flyer word for word but never ask whether the flyer is how that community learns about services. Each of these may be well intended. Each rests on the assumption that what works for the people who designed it will work for everyone.

Noticing this is different from accusing anyone. A useful habit is to shift from "Are we being fair?" to "What does this process assume?" Ask what a person has to already know, have or be comfortable with to succeed in it. Ask who tested it. Ask who has stopped showing up, or who succeeds only after extra help from a staff member who happens to share their background. Those informal workarounds are often a sign that the default fits some people better than others.

The DHS Equity Policy calls for the department to operate as a multicultural and intercultural organization and to use the Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions with lasting impact. The toolkit asks who a decision affects and whether affected communities were engaged. Those questions are one of the most practical tools for noticing team Minimization, because they move attention from intentions to effects. Use them on routine practices, not only on big policy changes.
lessons.keyPoint: Look for Minimization in routines, not just in attitudes. A process that is the same for everyone can still be built around one cultural pattern; ask what it assumes and who it was tested with.
lessons.example: Fictional case: A DSD grants team uses the same scoring rubric for every community organization applying for outreach funds. Applications are scored on a written narrative, a logic model and prior grant experience. Over several rounds, most awards go to larger agencies that have grant writers. Tomasz, a program consultant, hears from two small organizations serving newer immigrant communities that they did strong outreach work last year but could not describe it in the rubric's format. The team lead, Renee, says the rubric is fair because every applicant sees the same criteria.
lessons.question: What should Tomasz suggest to the team?
choices: Leave the rubric as is, because identical criteria are the definition of fairness.
Quietly help the two small organizations rewrite their narratives so they fit the existing format better.

Propose that the team use the Equity Analysis Toolkit to examine what the rubric assumes about applicants, and test options such as an oral application route, with any change reviewed through the grants and contracts process.
feedback: Identical criteria establish consistent treatment, not that the process measures the outreach skills it is meant to fund. This is Minimization at the level of a process.
Helping individual applicants is kind, but it leaves the default in place and depends on who knows Tomasz. The pattern will repeat next round.

This is the strongest response. It treats the rubric as a practice to examine, uses the department's own method, and routes any change through the people responsible for grant rules rather than making an informal exception.
lessons.reflection: Which routine in your unit do people describe as "just how we do it"? Who designed it, and whose way of working does it fit most easily?
lessons.action: Choose one team routine, such as a meeting format, intake step or review process. List who has to adapt to it and who does not, and bring one practice-focused question about it to your next team meeting.

check.question: Which statement best describes Minimization at the level of an organization?
check.correct: Treating rules and routines as culturally neutral because they apply to everyone, which can hide the fact that they were built around one group's patterns.
wrong: Refusing to serve people from certain cultural groups.
Openly stating that one culture's ways are better than others.
check.feedback: Refusing service or ranking cultures points to the more monocultural orientations earlier on the continuum. Minimization is subtler: the organization means well and applies the same rules to everyone, but does not notice that the rules carry a cultural pattern of their own.

lessons.title: Finding your own Minimization honestly
objectives: Identify personal phrases and habits that signal an emphasis on sameness in your own work.
Distinguish reflection on your own patterns from self-scoring or placing yourself on the continuum.
Explain why cultural self-understanding is a key step for people whose culture shapes the institution's defaults.
Plan one low-risk way to test an assumption you have been treating as universal.
lessons.teaching:
Most people who care about fairness find some Minimization in themselves when they look honestly. That is not a confession. It usually reflects a sincere commitment to treating people well, paired with a gap in seeing how culture shapes one's own habits. The continuum describes one form of Minimization as limited cultural self-understanding: when your own ways of communicating, deciding and showing respect feel like plain common sense, it is hard to see them as cultural at all. The first move, then, is not learning more about other groups. It is learning to see your own patterns as patterns.

Some useful questions to sit with privately. When I say someone is "unprofessional," what exact behavior am I describing, and where did I learn that standard? When a meeting goes well, whose participation style made it feel that way? When I say "I don't see color" or "I treat everyone the same," what am I hoping to communicate, and what might the other person hear? When a person served does not follow the plan, is my first explanation about them, or about the fit between the plan and their life? These questions are not a test, and there are no scores.

It helps to be honest about why Minimization feels good. It lowers conflict, it feels generous, and it fits public service values like consistency and equal treatment. Some staff, especially those from non-dominant groups, may also have learned to emphasize commonality because it made workplaces easier to navigate. That is a reasonable strategy and nobody else gets to decide it is wrong for you. If this describes you, the question is simply whether the strategy is still serving you and the people you work with, or whether it costs you something to keep your own perspective quiet.

A caution: reflection is not self-assessment on the inventory. Reading about an orientation and thinking "that sounds like me" is not an Intercultural Development Inventory result, and it should not be written into a development plan, performance review or team discussion as if it were. The inventory is administered only by Qualified Administrators and includes a debrief for good reason. What you can do on your own is notice specific habits, test them, and ask for feedback on specific behavior. That is the practical work, and it does not require anyone to name a stage.
lessons.keyPoint: Finding your own Minimization starts with seeing your habits as cultural rather than as simply normal. Reflect on specific behaviors and test them; do not score yourself or anyone else.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Dana, a case management supervisor, prides herself on running every team huddle the same way: quick updates, direct questions, decisions in the room. In a check-in, a newer case manager, Abdi, mentions he often has concerns about a case plan but raises them by email afterward because the huddle moves too fast. Dana's first reaction is that the format is fair because everyone gets the same airtime. Later she wonders whether "quick and direct" is simply her own preferred style.
lessons.question: What is the most useful next step for Dana?
choices: Ask the whole team, through a short anonymous or written option, what helps them raise concerns, and try one change such as sharing cases a day ahead.
Tell Abdi that he needs to speak up more in huddles, since that is the professional expectation.
Decide she is in Minimization and sign up the team for an intercultural assessment so she can see everyone's results.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Dana treats her format as one style among several, asks for input in a way that does not single Abdi out, and tests a specific change.
This assumes Dana's style is the neutral standard and puts all of the adjustment on Abdi. It also risks losing the concerns he has been raising, which matter for case quality.
Self-labeling is not an assessment result, and team members' inventory results are not a supervisor's to see or use. Any assessment should be voluntary and handled by a Qualified Administrator.
lessons.reflection: What is one habit of yours that you have always thought of as simply professional? Where did you learn it, and in what setting might it come across differently than you intend?
lessons.action: This week, choose one work habit, such as how you give feedback or run a meeting. Ask one trusted colleague how it lands for them, listen without defending it, and write down one thing you learned.

check.question: Why is cultural self-understanding especially important for people whose culture shapes an institution's defaults?
check.correct: Because their own ways of working can feel like neutral common sense, which makes it harder to notice the cultural assumptions built into the institution.
wrong: Because they are more biased than other people and need correction.
Because learning facts about other cultures is not useful.
check.feedback: The issue is visibility, not moral worth. When the institution already fits you, its patterns are easy to miss. Learning about other cultures still helps, but without seeing your own patterns you may treat new information as exceptions to a norm that is actually yours.

lessons.title: What actually helps people and teams move through Minimization
objectives: Explain why more reminders of shared values do not by themselves help people move past Minimization.
Identify practices that build cultural self-awareness and attention to difference, alongside commonality.
Plan a team practice that holds similarity and difference together in a real DHS or DSD decision.
Distinguish supportive development from pressure, labeling or public comparison.
lessons.teaching:
If Minimization is built on commonality, it might seem that the way forward is to throw commonality out. That is not the lesson. Bennett describes the resolution of this orientation as holding similarity and difference together: assuming similarity can help us appreciate difference, and a shared purpose gives difference a focus. The movement toward Acceptance happens when people keep their commitment to shared values while becoming able to see that the same value, such as respect or independence, is lived out differently in different cultural communities.

What helps? First, cultural self-awareness practices: comparing how members of a team were taught to show respect, disagree, ask for help or make a family decision, and noticing the range inside the room. Second, deliberate attention to difference in real work, not just in training: asking during a policy review how a rule would play out for people whose family structure, language or faith practice differs from the drafter's. Third, contact and listening done well: engaging community partners and people served as advisers, paid for their time where possible, rather than as audiences. Fourth, feedback on specific behavior over time, so people see the effect of their habits rather than being told what category they are in.

What does not help? Shaming people for emphasizing commonality usually pushes them back toward defending their position. Public comparisons of who is further along turn development into a competition and can harm colleagues from non-dominant groups who have used commonality to get by. Requiring people to share personal stories of discrimination or identity to prove a point asks for disclosure no one owes. And one-time training followed by nothing tends to fade. Development on the continuum is gradual, and the inventory's own materials describe individual development plans built after a debrief, not quick fixes.

For leaders, the most useful move is to change defaults. Build a question about cultural assumptions into the standard review of forms and notices. Test drafts with people who were not in the drafting room. Use the Equity Analysis Toolkit on routine decisions. When a team sees that noticing difference leads to better notices, fewer missed appointments and more trust from county and Tribal partners, attention to difference stops feeling like a threat to fairness and starts looking like part of doing the job well. Formal matters such as discrimination concerns or accommodation requests still go to EOAD, Human Resources or the ADA coordinator.
lessons.keyPoint: Moving through Minimization means keeping shared values while learning to see how culture shapes the ways they are lived. Change defaults and practice attention to difference; do not shame, rank or label people.
lessons.example: Fictional case: After a policy workgroup finishes a draft notice about changes to a waiver service, the lead, Priya, adds a new step before sign-off. Two team members read the notice aloud and ask, for each paragraph, what a reader would need to already know to act on it. The team also asks three members of a community advisory group, paid through an existing contract, to review it. One adviser, Lwin, says the notice assumes families will call a phone number during business hours, which many working parents in his community cannot do. Olu, a longtime team member, grumbles that the old notice was "the same for everyone."
lessons.question: How should Priya respond to Olu?
choices: Tell Olu that his comment shows the team still has work to do on its intercultural development.
Agree that the notice is the same for everyone, and explain that the review is checking whether everyone can actually act on it, then show him Lwin's specific finding.
Drop the new review step to keep the peace, since the old notice met legal requirements.
feedback: This labels Olu rather than addressing his concern and is likely to make him defensive about future reviews.
This is the strongest response. It affirms the commonality Olu values, reframes the goal as usable access for all, and grounds the change in a concrete finding rather than a lecture.
Meeting a minimum is not the same as working for the people receiving the notice. Dropping the step would lose useful information the team just gained.
lessons.reflection: What is one shared value you hold strongly at work? How might two people who both hold that value put it into practice differently?
lessons.action: Add one question to a review checklist you already use: "What would a person need to already know, have or be comfortable with to use this, and who have we checked that with?" Use it on your next draft.

check.question: According to Bennett's description, what does moving past Minimization involve?
check.correct: Holding similarity and difference together, so shared values provide focus while cultural differences in how they are lived are recognized.
wrong: Rejecting the idea that people share any common values.
Memorizing facts about as many cultural groups as possible.
check.feedback: Moving past Minimization does not mean abandoning commonality. It means holding similarity and difference at the same time. Cultural knowledge can help, but facts alone often get filed as exceptions to one's own norm unless self-awareness grows too.

cards.back: On the Intercultural Development Continuum, the transitional orientation that emphasizes commonality through human similarity and universal values, which can mask deeper cultural difference.
The belief that people share the same basic needs underneath cultural differences. True at one level, but it can hide how culture shapes the way needs are experienced and met.
The belief that certain values and principles apply everywhere and can be used to judge any situation, often without noticing that one's own interpretation of them is cultural.
Minimization's position between the monocultural mindsets of Denial and Polarization and the intercultural mindsets of Acceptance and Adaptation.
A person licensed to administer the Intercultural Development Inventory and share results. This program does not administer the inventory or guess anyone's result.

aid.heading: Spot Minimization in team practice
items: Ask what a process assumes a person already knows, has or is comfortable with.
Ask who designed and tested the form, notice, meeting format or rubric.
Notice informal workarounds and who needs them to succeed.
Use the Equity Analysis Toolkit questions on routine decisions, not only major policy changes.

aid.heading: Reflect on your own habits
items: Name a specific behavior you call professional or normal and ask where you learned it.
Ask for feedback on one behavior, not on your identity or orientation.
Treat reflection as private learning, never as a self-score on the continuum.

aid.heading: Support development without harm
items: Affirm shared values, then ask how they are lived out differently.
Change defaults such as review steps and testing with people served.
Never label, rank or publicly compare colleagues' orientations.
Do not require personal disclosure about identity or experience.
Send formal concerns to EOAD, Human Resources or the ADA coordinator.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Source for the continuum's orientations, Minimization as a transitional mindset, similarity and universalism, and the two forms of commonality emphasis in dominant and non-dominant groups. Used for shared vocabulary only; the program does not assess anyone.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — Why the IDI
sources.note: Confirms that the inventory is based on the continuum and can only be administered and its results shared by a licensed Qualified Administrator.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — How Individuals Use the IDI
sources.note: Describes the Qualified Administrator, the individual debrief and the Intercultural Development Plan. Supports the course's point that development follows a debrief rather than self-labeling.

sources.title: Intercultural Development Research Institute — Milton J. Bennett, Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity (encyclopedia entry, 2017)
sources.note: Bennett's description of Minimization, the organizational tendency to mask dominant culture privilege behind equal opportunity, and resolution by holding similarity and difference together. The DMIS is the earlier model from which the continuum was developed.

sources.title: International Journal of Intercultural Relations — Hammer, Bennett and Wiseman, Measuring intercultural sensitivity: The Intercultural Development Inventory (2003)
sources.note: Research article on the development of the fifty-item inventory from Bennett's model. Cited for background on the instrument, not to support any use of it by this program.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Equity Policy (2023)
sources.note: States the department's commitment to operate as a multicultural and intercultural organization and requires equity analysis for decisions with lasting impact. Supports the course's workplace applications.
